It reports 221 confirmed hits and 54 compounds with in-vitro therapeutic index above 6, including compounds classified as early- or late-stage inhibitors. The study proposes relevance to wider coronaviruses, including COVID-19, but reports no SARS-CoV-2-specific assay or human outcome and explicitly calls for additional mechanistic, in-vivo, synergism, and animal-efficacy validation.
Do not treat MERS-CoV inhibition in Vero cells, therapeutic-index values, or time-of-addition patterns as evidence of SARS-CoV-2 treatment efficacy. Future comparisons should test whether candidate effects reproduce against SARS-CoV-2, remain selective after toxicity and assay controls, occur in relevant human systems, and translate to controlled clinical outcomes.
The supplied source is abstract-only. It reports that mucosal aminoglycosides increased resistance to herpes simplex, influenza A, and Zika infections, reduced viral replication in primary human cells, protected germ-free mice, and induced ISG transcripts through TLR3, TRIF, IRF3, and IRF7, with recruitment of XCR1+ dendritic cells. No SARS-CoV-2-specific experiment, respiratory outcome, clinical benefit, or safety result is supplied.
Treat aminoglycoside-associated antiviral protection as a host-response hypothesis, not evidence of a COVID-19 treatment or preventive intervention. Future interpretation should distinguish microbiota-independent innate signaling from direct antiviral activity and require SARS-CoV-2-specific, respiratory, pharmacologic, toxicity, and clinical evidence.

sourceKnowledge:
The supplied full-text preprint examined 87 Cameroon fruit bats, recovered five near-complete RVA genomes, and identified highly divergent novel genotypes and reassortment. Several novel VP7/VP4 segments were predicted to evade routine human screening primers. Screening 25 nearby infants found RVA infections, but sequencing did not indicate bat-to-human transmission; the authors state that further human epidemiology is needed to assess human gastroenteritis potential. This is comparative rotavirus surveillance evidence, not direct SARS-CoV-2 evidence.
Separate assay detectability, viral diversity, ecological proximity, and confirmed spillover. Novel wildlife-virus sequences can expose surveillance blind spots, but human positivity near an animal reservoir does not establish interspecies transmission without sequence linkage and epidemiological support.
A complete-text MERS-CoV study sampled 479 people in Moroccan camel-herding regions. Four sera were positive or borderline by neutralisation screening; three had PRNT90 confirmation and one was borderline by PRNT50. Seropositive participants had no history of severe pneumonia, and none had travelled outside Morocco. ELISA and neutralisation showed poor correlation, with low positive predictive value for ELISA in this population. The paper concludes that zoonotic infection occurred but states that whether circulating African strains cause severe zoonotic disease remains unknown.
For coronavirus human-interaction studies, separate serological evidence of infection from severe disease, infectious shedding, and onward transmission. Assay concordance and confirmatory neutralisation matter: screening reactivity alone can substantially overstate confirmed infection. Comparative MERS evidence can guide surveillance questions for SARS-CoV-2, but does not establish SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis, transmission, treatment, or vaccine performance.
A non-peer-reviewed preprint reports that ACE2-Ig and catalytically attenuated mACE2-Ig bound SARS-CoV and 2019-nCoV receptor-binding domains and inhibited spike-pseudotyped viruses and spike-mediated cell fusion in vitro. The source presents these as potential diagnostic, prophylactic, or therapeutic applications, not established clinical outcomes. It also notes rapid clearance of native recombinant ACE2 and raises systemic cardiovascular effects as a safety concern.
Keep entry-assay inhibition distinct from treatment or prevention efficacy. For ACE2-based candidates, subsequent published evidence should compare activity against authentic virus with human-relevant safety, exposure, distribution, and clinical or validated translational outcomes; none of those outcomes is established by this preprint.
knowledge:
• A bat study found several previously unrecognized rotavirus forms and possible gaps in routine testing. Infections in nearby infants were detected, but the evidence did not show bat-to-human transmission.
• A camel-region study found evidence of some past MERS-CoV infections without severe pneumonia. Screening tests and confirmatory tests did not always agree, so a positive screening result alone may overstate infection.
• An early laboratory study found that ACE2-based decoys blocked related coronavirus entry in cell-based tests. This does not show that they work as treatments or prevent infection in people, and possible body-wide side effects remain uncertain.
next:
• We will investigate whether gastrointestinal SARS-CoV-2 findings represent active infectious virus and whether they are linked to transmission, rather than treating RNA or antigen detection alone as proof.
• We will compare broad wildlife-virus screening with evidence for actual cross-species spread, keeping detection separate from confirmed spillover.
• We will assess how reliably SARS-CoV-2 antibody screening is confirmed by independent tests, and whether infection can be distinguished from severe disease and onward transmission.
• We will review whether ACE2-based decoys work against authentic virus in human-relevant systems and whether their persistence, distribution, and safety support further development. These remain planned evidence reviews, not performed experiments.

The supplied abstract-only TGE coronavirus study compared five serological techniques in 24 infected and non-infected pig sera. Seroneutralisation, ELISA with purified virus, and VELCIA detected all infected sera, while several ELISA methods produced false positives; specificity differed substantially among assays, and VELCIA matched seroneutralisation specificity. This supports assay-comparison and orthogonal-confirmation priorities but is not direct SARS-CoV-2 evidence.
Serological reactivity should not automatically be treated as confirmed infection or immunity. In the supplied related-coronavirus study, assay choice changed specificity and false-positive results, motivating SARS-CoV-2 comparisons that report confirmatory neutralisation, assay thresholds, and prevalence context. The source is abstract-only and provides no SARS-CoV-2 clinical or vaccine findings.
The supplied abstract-only clinical study of nine hospitalized cases found predominantly upper-respiratory disease, high early swab RT-PCR sensitivity, live-virus isolates from swabs during the first illness week, and evidence of active upper-respiratory replication from subgenomic viral RNA. Viral RNA shedding outlasted symptoms and was reported in stool, while seroconversion occurred after about one week. The study suggests that RNA detection after symptom resolution or in stool should not automatically be interpreted as infectiousness or transmission.
For SARS-CoV-2 transmission research, distinguish upper-respiratory replication and early viable-virus recovery from later RNA shedding. Published comparisons should integrate culture or other infectivity evidence, timing relative to symptoms, specimen type, and epidemiological linkage; this abstract alone does not establish fecal-oral transmission or the infectious duration of stool RNA.

sourceKnowledge:
An abstract-only living systematic review and meta-analysis included 79 SARS-CoV-2 studies, alongside SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV comparisons. It reported mean RNA-shedding durations of 17.0 days in the upper respiratory tract, 14.6 in the lower respiratory tract, 17.2 in stool, and 16.6 in serum; maximum reported durations were 83, 59, 35, and 60 days, respectively. No included study detected live virus beyond illness day nine, despite persistently high viral loads. Upper-respiratory viral load appeared to peak during the first week, around symptom onset to day five.
